prize_parts.citation: for the theory and first experimental realisation of strong coupling between single microwave photons and superconducting artificial atoms on a chip, establishing circuit quantum electrodynamics

statement.case_for: Circuit QED opened a regime that was not accessible before: strong, tunable coupling between an engineered atom and a single microwave mode, with dispersive quantum non-demolition readout and quantum-limited amplification. The 2004 theory proposal (Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin, Schoelkopf) and the 2004 strong-coupling experiment (Wallraff, Schoelkopf and co-workers) form a clean theory-plus-experiment pairing. Two decades of reproduction in dozens of laboratories, and on several qubit types (Cooper-pair box, transmon, fluxonium), show that the physics is robust. It is also the basis of microwave quantum optics (artificial atoms in waveguides, photon routers, the dynamical Casimir effect). The discovery being rewarded is the control of single quantum systems in a circuit, not the quantum computer, which is still ahead of us. I rank it first because I know the field in detail and can judge that the claim of a new regime is real.
statement.case_against: The 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits has just honoured the neighbouring foundation, and the committee may feel that a circuit prize a year later is too close, or that circuit QED is mainly the enabling architecture for others. Credit is also hard to cut at three: Girvin and Huang were co-authors of the 2004 proposal, and the Yale and ETH groups shared the experimental work. Finally, I am the member closest to this field, so my ranking should be discounted until others have judged whether the discovery stands on its own physics.

responses.point: Kroll ranks circuit QED third and calls it a reliable device platform, but warns that the transmon and Josephson-circuit work recognised in 2025 may complicate how it is framed, and that the 2025 prize partly overlaps.
responses.response: I take the overlap seriously, but I think it is smaller than it looks. The 2025 citation concerns macroscopic quantum tunnelling and energy quantisation in a Josephson circuit, which showed that a circuit variable behaves quantum mechanically. Circuit QED is a different discovery: coupling that circuit coherently to a single photon in a resonator, with dispersive readout. The 2025 laureates did not do this. Where I agree with Kroll is that the citation must say strong light-matter coupling and not simply superconducting qubits. I would also say that if the committee feels one circuit prize in consecutive years is too much, that is a legitimate argument about timing, and not about merit.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks circuit QED last of his ranked entries because the 2025 prize has just recognised the nearby foundation, and he notes that credit is shared and hard to cut at three, with Girvin and Huang partly absent.
responses.response: The credit problem is real and I do not wish to hide it. Girvin and Huang were on the 2004 proposal, and the three-person limit is painful. My reasoning is that Blais carried the proposal and the detailed theory, while Wallraff and Schoelkopf gave the experimental demonstration; this is the cut the field itself usually makes. I disagree that this is a reason to rank the topic last. A difficult allocation of credit would be a reason to design the citation carefully, not to say the discovery is of low value. On his timing worry I partly concede: if the committee prefers a gap after 2025, then B041 is my next choice.

responses.point: Lindroth puts optical lattice clocks first, because the precision rests on understanding atomic structure, the physics is confirmed by many laboratories, and the two-person configuration is natural.
responses.response: I agree that B041 is a very strong and clean candidate, and the agreement of lattice clocks across continents at the 1e-18 level is exactly the independent reproducibility I look for. My reservations are about novelty of regime and overlap. Lattice clocks continue the line of the 2005 prize (frequency combs, Hall and Hänsch) and the 2012 prize (Wineland, ion control), and Ye has a role in the comb work as well. I do not think that disqualifies it. It is my first alternative, and I would not argue strongly against it if the committee settles there.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks topological insulators first as a prediction later confirmed by nature, noting that Mele's omission is uncomfortable and that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang also matter for the HgTe proposal.
responses.response: Outside my own field I defer, but the arc he describes, with theory predicting the quantum spin Hall state and Molenkamp's HgTe wells confirming it, is persuasive and fits the same prediction-then-confirmation criterion that I apply to circuit QED. My question is the one he raises himself: with Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Bernevig, Zhang and Hasan all with a claim, can the committee find a three-person configuration that is not arbitrary? Circuit QED has the same difficulty, so I do not want to use that against B032; I only suggest it should be tested as hard as mine.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards circuit QED as sufficiently distinct from the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits to be timely so soon afterwards.
Whether the allocation among Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf is defensible without Girvin and Huang, who co-authored the 2004 proposal.
Whether the discovery would be judged mainly as an enabling architecture for quantum computing rather than as a new physical regime of light-matter interaction.
How much weight B041 deserves given that it has the broadest support and none of the overlap concerns about the 2025 prize, against its continuity with the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
statement.conflict_note: Possible recusal issue: I lead the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work in the same Chalmers superconducting-circuit community as the circuit QED candidates; my own research on waveguide QED and microwave quantum optics is closely related to B031, and I rank it first. I have no personal connection to Blais, Wallraff or Schoelkopf that I can identify from my profile, but the committee should decide whether my advocacy for B031 requires disclosure or recusal. I have no specific conflict with B041, B018 or the other shortlisted candidates.
